text: A flash loan lets you borrow an arbitrary amount of capital with zero collateral, as long as you repay it plus a small fee within the same transaction — otherwise the whole transaction reverts, as if it never happened. That removes capital as a constraint: an attacker who'd normally need millions to move a market can borrow those millions for about fifteen seconds and walk away with whatever profit the manipulation created.

Harvest Finance's vaults calculated their share price directly from the current, on-chain exchange rate inside a Curve pool — a spot price, set entirely by whatever was sitting in that pool's reserves at that exact moment. That's the entire vulnerability: a price read straight from a source a single transaction could move.

On October 26th, 2020, the attacker borrowed USDC and USDT via a flash loan, dumped stablecoins into the Curve pool to skew its price, deposited into the Harvest vault while the pool was distorted so the deposit bought far more vault shares than it should, traded back to restore the pool, then withdrew at close to the correct rate and repaid the loan — keeping the difference. Harvest's own post-mortem put the loss at $33.8 million.

Nothing here was a reentrancy bug — every function call completed and returned normally. The fix isn't a one-line guard, it's a design decision about where a price is allowed to come from: a time-weighted average price, built from history across many blocks instead of one block's reserves, or an independent Chainlink feed sourced off the pool entirely. Both make the price source expensive or slow for an attacker to move.

The scariest part of this exploit is that the attacker never broke into anything — every transaction executed exactly as written. Next up: a case where the manipulated market is the oracle itself, and the attacker doesn't even need a flash loan — just capital, and time.
